title: Disentangling the Spread in Wind Projections Over Europe and the Impacts on Energy Generation
content:
Abstract

Future changes in near-surface wind speed currently display a large spread and uncertainty. A better understanding of future wind projections will enable the anticipation and enhancement of clean energy generation. Here, we provide insights on model spread over Europe employing a large ensemble of sub-daily bias-adjusted CMIP6 wind simulations, for the historical (1979–2014) and future (2041–2100) periods under different socio-economic scenarios. Europe is projected to experience a gradual weakening of near-surface wind speed, especially over central and southern regions during winter, and a strengthening in northern Europe and southern latitudes during summer. These changes typically intensify and become more spatially coherent by the late 21st century in the worst-case scenario (SSP585). Climate change may modestly enhance wind capacity factor (WCF) for energy generation in southern Europe (Iberia) during summer, while generally decreasing in the rest of Europe. During winter, WCF remains relatively stable (with decreases in Eastern Europe and northern latitudes) but is affected by larger uncertainty. Based on hierarchical clustering, sub-ensembles of models are constructed, showing differences not only in the magnitude and sign of WCF changes, but also in their regional heterogeneity. We show that uncertainty in wind speed and wind energy production is strongly shaped by model and scenario differences, and reinforce the need to account for the diurnal cycle and seasonal differences at a regional scale. Furthermore, strengthened NAO-WCF coupling and more positive mean NAO states may enhance northern European wind resources, while reduced variance could diminish year-to-year variability, important for long-term energy planning.
